summary: Measures GPU energy of multi-agent SWE systems (HyperAgent, BOAD) on locally served Qwen3.6 models and attributes per-turn energy to token categories, finding output tokens cost 30-1,000x more energy than input/cached tokens. Proposes 'Librarian', a persistent, lookup-only code-search sub-agent that returns file:line pointers instead of excerpts and is told which ranges were edited since its last call; it cuts per-episode GPU energy 11-30% at non-inferior pass rate on SWE-Bench Verified and a 100-task SWE-Bench-Live sample.

claims.claim: Output tokens cost 30-1,000x more GPU energy per token than uncached/cached input tokens.
claims.evidence: Table 2: beta_o 967 vs beta_u 30.5 vs beta_c 1.36 mJ/tok (A3B/A100); 3,512 vs 33.97 vs 2.04 (27B/B200); R^2 0.979-0.992; VIF<=1.05 (Table 10); fitted on 23k-196k turns (App. A.2).

claims.claim: Librarian reduces per-episode GPU energy of existing MAS by 11-30% while preserving pass rate.
claims.evidence: Table 4 (500 SWE-Bench Verified tasks): HyperAgent A3B 25.64->22.73 kJ (-11%), HyperAgent 27B 121.84->91.45 (-25%), BOAD A3B 17.45->14.66, BOAD 27B 88.96->71.76; pass rate equal or higher. Table 5 SWE-Bench-Live HyperAgent 182.32->128.26 (-30%) but pass 23->21. App. G Table 15: Wilcoxon significant in 7/8 cost comparisons after Holm; McNemar-style non-inferiority holds 8/8 at 3.5pt margin, only 5/8 at 2pt.

claims.claim: Re-exploration of overlapping file regions across sub-agent invocations is a major source of excess MAS output.
claims.evidence: Table 3 gives an explicit upper bound (not point estimate) on duplicate output, e.g. HyperAgent executor 26.8% cross-invocation from editor and 34.4% within-invocation; authors acknowledge it is a bound.

claims.claim: All four mechanisms (persistent session, pointer-only output, lookup-only scope, freshness report) contribute.
claims.evidence: Table 8 leave-one-out on 100 tasks, Qwen3.6-27B only: removing any mechanism raises output tokens and energy on both MAS; pass rates differ by 1-4 points on 100 tasks, which is within noise.

claims.claim: Persistent history beats BM25/dense retrieval of prior reads.
claims.evidence: Table 9: lowest energy in 3 of 4 settings; on BOAD/A3B dense retrieval wins on both pass (77 vs 74) and energy (12.42 vs 13.61). 100-task samples only.

patterns.note: A long-lived, lookup-only sub-agent isolated from editing reduces orchestrator context and output volume; evidence on two MAS x two backbones.
Table 1: single-agent Vanilla uses less energy (10.31 kJ A3B) than any MAS incl. BOAD+Librarian (14.66 kJ); Vanilla pass rate is never reported, so MAS benefit over a single agent is not established.
Pointer-only answers act as output compaction; LastNObservation truncation (observation masking) increased energy and lowered pass in every setting (Table 4).
Within-episode persistent search history with a freshness report of edited ranges; Figure 3 shows fewer turns per later invocation.
Librarian uses bash/grep + file view; compares against BM25 and embedding retrieval of prior reads (P06) with mixed results.
Shows API token counts/pricing are a poor proxy for energy; output-token budget is the lever. Directly relevant to cost caps.

methodology.sample: 500 SWE-Bench Verified tasks for main results; 100-task samples of SWE-Bench-Live (46 repos, 41 not in Verified), and 100-task samples for ablations/retrieval comparisons.
methodology.baselines: Two published MAS (HyperAgent, BOAD) as hosts; token-efficiency baselines caveman prompting and LastNObservation (N=5). No comparison to a commercial agent host; single-agent Vanilla pass rate not reported.
methodology.models: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.6-27B, FP8, vLLM on B200 (plus A100 for regression).
methodology.variance: One run per task; paired Wilcoxon (cost) and McNemar-style non-inferiority (pass) tests with Holm correction on the 500-task set (App. G). No repeated seeds.
methodology.ablations: Leave-one-out of four mechanisms (Table 8); persistent session transferred to executor role; retrieval variants (Table 9).
methodology.contamination_controls: None for SWE-Bench Verified; SWE-Bench-Live sample used as a fresher split.

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/ml-postech/Librarian; system prompt and tool policy in App. B.4-B.5.

biases.detail: SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Bench-Live are Python repositories only.
GPU energy is measured on self-hosted vLLM; teams paying per-token API prices see a different cost function (input tokens dominate billing, cached tokens discounted).

Ablations, retrieval comparison and SWE-Bench-Live use 100 tasks; HyperAgent A3B baseline pass is 66.0 on 500 tasks but 71.0 on the 100-task sample, showing sampling noise exceeds many reported deltas.
Main comparison omits the cheaper single-agent baseline's pass rate, so 'MAS + Librarian' is never shown to beat a plain single agent on cost-effectiveness.
Only 3B-27B active-parameter open models; authors concede transfer to >500B models is open.

verdict_reason: Headline numbers are reproducible from Tables 2, 4 and 5 and backed by paired significance tests with multiple-comparison correction. Main gaps: Python-only, small open models, one run per task, no single-agent pass-rate comparison. The design guidance (persistent lookup sub-agent, pointer-only returns, edited-range freshness report) transfers regardless of energy accounting.
applicability: For a Java team whose ingestion spans 4+ repositories, the transferable design is a single long-lived 'librarian' lookup sub-agent per task. It searches across all repos, returns repo/file:line pointers rather than pasted code, and gets a freshness report listing ranges edited since its last call. This directly targets cross-repo re-exploration, where content-model and delivery-API code is read repeatedly. It is host-agnostic: it works as a subagent definition in Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. Caveats: the evidence is Python on self-hosted models, so the energy savings are not dollar savings under per-token API pricing; savings come from output-token reduction, which is still the most expensive token class on most commercial APIs. Do not read this as evidence that multi-agent beats single-agent. Table 1 shows a single agent was cheapest. Avoid naive observation truncation (LastNObservation hurt both cost and pass rate).
